Set a random seed before each simulation question and report it. You may use standard packages unless a question asks you to write the calculation yourself. Use equal neighbor weights throughout. Here pp counts the covariates used to measure distance; do not add an intercept column to a KNN predictor matrix. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact simulation results need not agree.

Question 1: Estimate the bias and variance of KNN

In our previous homework, we used repeated simulations to study the behavior of linear regression estimators. We will now use the same idea for KNN. Consider the regression model

Yi=f(𝑿i)+ϵi,f(𝒙)=0.5x1+sin⁡(x2)−0.3x32, Y_i=f(\mathbf X_i)+\epsilon_i, \qquad f(\mathbf x)=0.5x_1+\sin(x_2)-0.3x_3^2,

where the three covariates are independent standard normal variables and ϵi∼𝒩(0,0.12)\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,0.1^2) independently of the covariates and other observations. Generate n=400n=400 training observations. Our goal is to estimate the mean response at

𝒙0=(0.5,0.7,1)𝖳. \mathbf x_0=(0.5,0.7,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Use Euclidean distance and consider k=1,3,5,…,29k=1,3,5,\ldots,29.

  1. Calculate f(𝒙0)f(\mathbf x_0). Generate one training dataset and obtain the KNN prediction at 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 for each value of kk.

• Solution:

The true mean response at 𝒙0=(0.5,0.7,1)𝖳\mathbf{x}_0=(0.5,0.7,1)^{\mathsf T} is

f(𝒙0)=0.5(0.5)+sin⁡(0.7)−0.3(1)2=0.5942. f(\mathbf{x}_0) =0.5(0.5)+\sin(0.7)-0.3(1)^2 =0.5942.

  1. Independently repeat the generation of the training covariates and responses 200 times. Within each repetition, use the same training data for every value of kk. Store the predictions in a matrix with 200 rows and one column for each value of kk. Use this matrix to estimate the bias, variance, and mean squared error of the estimated mean response. Use divisor 200 when calculating the empirical variance, and verify numerically that

mean squared error=squared bias+variance. \text{mean squared error} =\text{squared bias}+\text{variance}.

Plot squared bias, variance, and mean squared error against kk in one figure. Explain the pattern and compare it with the bias-variance trade-off for ridge regression or lasso.

• Solution:

Show the workflow 
set.seed(4322)
cat("Seed used: 4322\n")
Seed used: 4322
Show the workflow 
n = 400
B = 200
k.values = seq(1, 29, by = 2)
x0 = c(0.5, 0.7, 1)

f0 = 0.5 * x0[1] + sin(x0[2]) - 0.3 * x0[3]^2

pred.matrix = matrix(
  NA,
  nrow = B,
  ncol = length(k.values)
)

for (b in 1:B) {
  
  X = matrix(rnorm(n * 3), nrow = n, ncol = 3)
  
  f = 0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * X[, 3]^2
  y = f + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.1)
  
  distances = sqrt(rowSums((X - matrix(x0, n, 3, byrow = TRUE))^2))
  neighbor.order = order(distances)
  
  for (j in seq_along(k.values)) {
    k = k.values[j]
    pred.matrix[b, j] = mean(y[neighbor.order[1:k]])
  }
}

mean.pred = colMeans(pred.matrix)

bias = mean.pred - f0
bias.squared = bias^2

variance = colMeans(
  (pred.matrix - matrix(mean.pred, B, length(k.values), byrow = TRUE))^2
)

mse = colMeans((pred.matrix - f0)^2)

results = data.frame(
  k = k.values,
  squared.bias = bias.squared,
  variance = variance,
  mse = mse,
  bias2.plus.variance = bias.squared + variance
)

The numerical difference between MSE and squared bias plus variance is essentially zero, which verifies

MSE=Bias2+Variance. \text{MSE}=\text{Bias}^2+\text{Variance}.

As kk increases, each KNN prediction averages more observations. This generally lowers the variance because the prediction becomes less sensitive to individual training observations. At the same time, using more neighbors means averaging observations farther away from 𝒙0\mathbf{x}_0, so the squared bias tends to increase. The MSE balances these two effects and is usually lowest at an intermediate value of kk.

This is similar to ridge regression and lasso. A small kk gives a more flexible KNN fit with lower bias but higher variance. Increasing kk adds more smoothing, giving higher bias but lower variance. This is similar to increasing the penalty λ\lambda in ridge or lasso, which increases shrinkage and generally trades lower variance for higher bias.

Question 2: Compare KNN with lasso

Use the response model from Question 1, including the noise standard deviation 0.10.1, but generate p=30p=30 covariates. The response still depends only on the first three. Consider these two settings:

  • Setting 1: all 30 covariates are independent standard normal variables.

  • Setting 2: the covariates have a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol\Sigma, where

    Σjj=1,Σjl=0.8for j≠l. \Sigma_{jj}=1, \qquad \Sigma_{jl}=0.8\quad\text{for }j\ne l.

In each setting, generate 400 training observations and 1,000 independent test observations. Fit 5NN using Euclidean distance on the supplied covariate scale. All covariates already have population variance one.

For lasso, use a linear model containing the 30 covariates and a separately fitted, unpenalized intercept. Follow the Week 4 objective,

Lλ(𝜷)=12n∥𝒚̃−𝑿𝜷∥22+λ‖𝜷‖1, L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) =\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert \widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta \right\rVert_2^2 +\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1,

where 𝑿∈ℝn×30\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times30} contains the centered and standardized covariates and 𝒚̃\widetilde{\mathbf y} is the centered training response. Select the penalty by ten-fold cross-validation over 41 logarithmically spaced values from 10−410^{-4} to 11. Estimate all means and scales using only the training portion of each fold, with divisor equal to that portion’s sample size. After selecting the penalty, refit on all training observations and apply the fitted transformations unchanged to the test observations. Do not add nonlinear terms to the lasso model.

  1. Fit both methods in each setting. Use the same training and test data for the two methods within a setting. Report their test MSE values in one table, together with the selected lasso penalty and the number of nonzero lasso slopes. You only need to generate one dataset for each setting; repeated simulations are not required.

• Solution:

Show the workflow 
library(MASS)
library(kknn)
library(glmnet)
Loading required package: Matrix
Loaded glmnet 4.1-10
Show the workflow 
n_train = 400
n_test = 1000
p = 30
lambda_grid = 10^seq(0, -4, length.out = 41)

make_response = function(X) {
  0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * X[, 3]^2 +
    rnorm(nrow(X), mean = 0, sd = 0.1)
}

fit_methods = function(X, y) {
  
  colnames(X) = paste0("X", 1:p)
  
  X_train = X[1:n_train, ]
  X_test = X[(n_train + 1):(n_train + n_test), ]
  y_train = y[1:n_train]
  y_test = y[(n_train + 1):(n_train + n_test)]
  
  # 5NN with equal neighbor weights
  knn_train = data.frame(y = y_train, X_train)
  knn_test = data.frame(X_test)
  
  knn_fit = kknn(
    y ~ .,
    train = knn_train,
    test = knn_test,
    k = 5,
    kernel = "rectangular"
  )
  
  knn_pred = knn_fit$fitted.values
  knn_mse = mean((y_test - knn_pred)^2)
  
  # Ten balanced folds for lasso
  foldid = sample(rep(1:10, each = n_train / 10))
  
  lasso_cv = cv.glmnet(
    x = X_train,
    y = y_train,
    family = "gaussian",
    alpha = 1,
    lambda = lambda_grid,
    foldid = foldid,
    type.measure = "mse",
    standardize = TRUE,
    intercept = TRUE
  )
  
  selected_lambda = lasso_cv$lambda.min
  
  lasso_pred = as.numeric(
    predict(lasso_cv, newx = X_test, s = "lambda.min")
  )
  
  lasso_mse = mean((y_test - lasso_pred)^2)
  
  lasso_coef = as.numeric(
    coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.min")
  )
  
  nonzero_slopes = sum(lasso_coef[-1] != 0)
  
  c(
    knn_mse = knn_mse,
    lasso_mse = lasso_mse,
    lambda = selected_lambda,
    nonzero = nonzero_slopes
  )
}

# Setting 1: independent covariates
seed_setting1 = 43251
set.seed(seed_setting1)

X1 = matrix(
  rnorm((n_train + n_test) * p),
  nrow = n_train + n_test,
  ncol = p
)

y1 = make_response(X1)
result1 = fit_methods(X1, y1)

# Setting 2: correlated covariates
seed_setting2 = 43252
set.seed(seed_setting2)

Sigma = matrix(0.8, nrow = p, ncol = p)
diag(Sigma) = 1

X2 = MASS::mvrnorm(
  n = n_train + n_test,
  mu = rep(0, p),
  Sigma = Sigma
)

y2 = make_response(X2)
result2 = fit_methods(X2, y2)

cat("Setting 1 seed:", seed_setting1, "\n")
Setting 1 seed: 43251
Show the workflow 
cat("Setting 2 seed:", seed_setting2, "\n\n")
Setting 2 seed: 43252
Show the workflow 
results = data.frame(
  Setting = c("Setting 1", "Setting 2"),
  "5NN test MSE" = round(c(result1["knn_mse"],
                           result2["knn_mse"]), 4),
  "Lasso test MSE" = round(c(result1["lasso_mse"],
                             result2["lasso_mse"]), 4),
  "Selected lasso penalty" = round(c(result1["lambda"],
                                     result2["lambda"]), 6),
  "Nonzero lasso slopes" = c(result1["nonzero"],
                              result2["nonzero"]),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(results)
Setting 5NN test MSE Lasso test MSE Selected lasso penalty Nonzero lasso slopes
Setting 1 0.5508 0.2514 0.031623 9
Setting 2 0.1773 0.2160 0.019953 7
  1. Compare the results between the two settings. Explain how correlation can change the usefulness of Euclidean neighborhoods, and why lasso does not use all covariates in the same way as KNN.

• Solution:

The results show that 5NN works much better in the correlated setting than in the independent setting. When all 30 covariates are independent, the 27 covariates that do not directly affect the response still count equally in the Euclidean distance. This makes it harder for KNN to find observations that are actually close in the first three important covariates.

With strong correlation, many of the 30 covariates contain overlapping information instead of acting like 30 completely separate directions. This can make the Euclidean neighborhoods more useful and improve the 5NN predictions.

Lasso handles the extra covariates differently. Instead of using every covariate to measure distance, it applies a penalty to the slopes and can set many of them exactly to zero. Therefore, lasso can reduce the effect of unnecessary covariates, while KNN always uses all 30 covariates when deciding which observations are neighbors.

  1. The response model contains sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, but the lasso fit uses only linear terms. Explain how this difference affects the comparison. Would the results justify a general claim that correlation always helps KNN, or that one method is always better? Explain why.

• Solution:

The true response contains sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, but the lasso model only includes linear terms. This means the lasso model is not able to represent the true response function exactly. It can capture the linear effect of X1X_1 and can give a linear approximation to sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2), but it cannot directly capture the curved relationship from X32X_3^2.

KNN does not assume that the response is linear, so it can adapt to these nonlinear relationships when it is able to find useful nearby observations. However, KNN also has the disadvantage of using all 30 covariates in its distance calculation.

The results from these two datasets do not justify saying that correlation always helps KNN or that one method is always better. Correlation can change which observations appear close under Euclidean distance, and this can either help or hurt depending on the structure of the data. The comparison also depends on the sample size, number of covariates, value of kk, noise level, and the form of the true response function. Since only one dataset was generated for each setting, these results describe this simulation rather than a general rule.

Question 3: Observed dimension and latent dimension

The lecture’s handwritten digit example shows that KNN can work with many measured covariates. We will use a simulation to investigate why the structure of those covariates matters.

Let p=100p=100 be the number of observed covariates and let mm be the number of latent variables. For each observation, generate

𝑿i=𝑨𝒁i+𝜼i,Yi=Zi1+Zi2+ϵi, \mathbf X_i=\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i+\boldsymbol\eta_i, \qquad Y_i=Z_{i1}+Z_{i2}+\epsilon_i,

where 𝑨∈ℝ100×m\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{100\times m} has independent entries from Uniform[−2,2][-2,2]. The entries of 𝒁i∈ℝm\mathbf Z_i\in\mathbb R^m and 𝜼i∈ℝ100\boldsymbol\eta_i\in\mathbb R^{100}, and the scalar ϵi\epsilon_i, are independent standard normal variables, also independent of 𝑨\mathbf A. Generate 𝑨\mathbf A once and use it for all training and test observations in that dataset.

Compare m=3m=3 and m=30m=30. In each setting, generate 200 training observations and 200 independent test observations. Fit KNN using only the 100 observed covariates in 𝑿\mathbf X, with Euclidean distance on their generated scale. The latent variables in 𝒁\mathbf Z are used to generate the data but are not available to the fitted model. Consider k=2,10,18,…,82k=2,10,18,\ldots,82.

  1. Generate one dataset for each value of mm. Fit KNN for every value of kk and calculate test MSE. Within a setting, use the same training and test observations for all values of kk.

• Solution:

Show the workflow 
library(FNN)

seed = 43253
set.seed(seed)
cat("Seed:", seed, "\n")
Seed: 43253
Show the workflow 
p = 100
n_train = 200
n_test = 200
k_values = seq(2, 82, by = 8)

generate_data = function(m) {
  
  A = matrix(runif(p * m, min = -2, max = 2),
             nrow = p, ncol = m)
  
  Z_train = matrix(rnorm(n_train * m),
                   nrow = n_train, ncol = m)
  Z_test = matrix(rnorm(n_test * m),
                  nrow = n_test, ncol = m)
  
  eta_train = matrix(rnorm(n_train * p),
                     nrow = n_train, ncol = p)
  eta_test = matrix(rnorm(n_test * p),
                    nrow = n_test, ncol = p)
  
  X_train = Z_train %*% t(A) + eta_train
  X_test = Z_test %*% t(A) + eta_test
  
  y_train = Z_train[, 1] + Z_train[, 2] + rnorm(n_train)
  y_test = Z_test[, 1] + Z_test[, 2] + rnorm(n_test)
  
  list(
    X_train = X_train,
    X_test = X_test,
    y_train = y_train,
    y_test = y_test
  )
}

knn_mse = function(data, k) {
  
  pred = FNN::knn.reg(
    train = data$X_train,
    test = data$X_test,
    y = data$y_train,
    k = k
  )$pred
  
  mean((data$y_test - pred)^2)
}

data_m3 = generate_data(m = 3)
data_m30 = generate_data(m = 30)

mse_m3 = sapply(k_values, function(k) knn_mse(data_m3, k))
mse_m30 = sapply(k_values, function(k) knn_mse(data_m30, k))

results = data.frame(
  k = k_values,
  `Test MSE (m = 3)` = mse_m3,
  `Test MSE (m = 30)` = mse_m30,
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(results, digits = 4)

These curves compare the specified choices of kk in a controlled simulation; they are not a cross-validation procedure for selecting a final model.

• Solution:

Show the workflow 
library(FNN)
library(ggplot2)
Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.4.3
Show the workflow 
seed = 43254
set.seed(seed)
cat("Seed:", seed, "\n")
Seed: 43254
Show the workflow 
p = 100
n_train = 200
n_test = 200
k_values = seq(2, 82, by = 8)
B = 50

run_one_dataset = function(m) {
  
  A = matrix(runif(p * m, min = -2, max = 2),
             nrow = p, ncol = m)
  
  Z_train = matrix(rnorm(n_train * m),
                   nrow = n_train, ncol = m)
  Z_test = matrix(rnorm(n_test * m),
                  nrow = n_test, ncol = m)
  
  eta_train = matrix(rnorm(n_train * p),
                     nrow = n_train, ncol = p)
  eta_test = matrix(rnorm(n_test * p),
                    nrow = n_test, ncol = p)
  
  X_train = Z_train %*% t(A) + eta_train
  X_test = Z_test %*% t(A) + eta_test
  
  y_train = Z_train[, 1] + Z_train[, 2] + rnorm(n_train)
  y_test = Z_test[, 1] + Z_test[, 2] + rnorm(n_test)
  
  sapply(k_values, function(k) {
    
    pred = FNN::knn.reg(
      train = X_train,
      test = X_test,
      y = y_train,
      k = k
    )$pred
    
    mean((y_test - pred)^2)
  })
}

mse_m3 = matrix(0, nrow = B, ncol = length(k_values))
mse_m30 = matrix(0, nrow = B, ncol = length(k_values))

for (b in 1:B) {
  mse_m3[b, ] = run_one_dataset(m = 3)
  mse_m30[b, ] = run_one_dataset(m = 30)
}

average_results = data.frame(
  k = rep(k_values, 2),
  Average_MSE = c(colMeans(mse_m3), colMeans(mse_m30)),
  m = factor(
    rep(c(3, 30), each = length(k_values)),
    labels = c("m = 3", "m = 30")
  )
)

ggplot(
  average_results,
  aes(x = k, y = Average_MSE, color = m)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "k",
    y = "Average test MSE",
    color = "Latent dimension"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

These curves show the average test MSE over 50 independently generated datasets for each latent dimension. They compare the given values of kk and are not being used as a cross-validation procedure for selecting a final model.

  1. Both settings have 100 observed covariates, and the response depends on only two latent variables. Explain why their KNN performance can still differ. What role does the noise 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i play, and why are the observed data not confined exactly to an mm-dimensional linear space?

• Solution:

Even though both settings have 100 observed covariates and YY depends only on Z1Z_1 and Z2Z_2, their KNN performance can differ because the observed covariates contain different amounts of latent information.

When m=3m=3, the 100 observed covariates are mainly mixtures of only three latent variables. Two of those latent variables directly affect the response, so Euclidean distance in 𝑿\mathbf X is more likely to reflect differences that are useful for predicting YY.

When m=30m=30, the observed covariates contain information from 30 latent variables, but only Z1Z_1 and Z2Z_2 affect the response. The other 28 latent variables still affect Euclidean distance even though they do not directly help predict YY. This can make it harder for KNN to find neighbors that are actually similar in the response-relevant directions.

The noise 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i also changes the geometry. Without this noise,

𝑿i=𝑨𝒁i \mathbf X_i=\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i

would lie in the column space of 𝑨\mathbf A, which has dimension at most mm. However, the added noise 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i has independent components in all 100 observed directions. Therefore, each observation is pushed away from the exact latent subspace.

So the observed data have an underlying low-dimensional structure, but they are not confined exactly to an mm-dimensional linear space. This helps explain why the latent dimension and the added noise can strongly affect how useful Euclidean neighborhoods are for KNN.

Question 4: Classify handwritten digits

Use zip.train and zip.test from the R package ElemStatLearn, as in the lecture. The package has been retired from the active CRAN repository. If needed, install the archived package into your usual R library, then load the two datasets. Python users can use the course copies of the same training data and test data. These compressed CSV files have no headers and are included in the homework ZIP under data/knn. Run the Python code from the folder containing data.

Each image has 16×16=25616\times16=256 pixel values. The first column is the digit label and the remaining columns are the pixel values. Use the first 1,000 rows of zip.train and the first 500 rows of zip.test. Use the original pixel values without standardization, and do not include the digit label in a distance calculation.

For a test image 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 and a training image 𝒙i\mathbf x_i, the two distances are

dE(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256(x0j−xij)2,dM(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256|x0j−xij|. d_E(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{256}(x_{0j}-x_{ij})^2}, \qquad d_M(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sum_{j=1}^{256}|x_{0j}-x_{ij}|.

  1. Write a 5NN classification function that allows either Euclidean or Manhattan distance. For each test image, calculate its distances to the training images directly, find the five nearest, and return the most frequent digit label. Break distance ties by the smaller training row number and voting ties by the smallest digit. Do not use a built-in distance or KNN function for this part.

• Solution:

Show the workflow 
library(ElemStatLearn)

data(zip.train)
data(zip.test)

train_data = zip.train[1:1000, ]
test_data = zip.test[1:500, ]

train_y = train_data[, 1]
test_y = test_data[, 1]

train_x = as.matrix(train_data[, -1])
test_x = as.matrix(test_data[, -1])

knn5_classify = function(train_x, train_y, test_x,
                         distance = c("euclidean", "manhattan")) {
  
  distance = match.arg(distance)
  predictions = numeric(nrow(test_x))
  
  for (i in 1:nrow(test_x)) {
    
    difference = sweep(train_x, 2, test_x[i, ], "-")
    
    if (distance == "euclidean") {
      d = sqrt(rowSums(difference^2))
    } else {
      d = rowSums(abs(difference))
    }
    
    # Distance ties are broken by smaller training row number
    neighbor_order = order(d, seq_along(d))
    neighbor_labels = train_y[neighbor_order[1:5]]
    
    # Count votes for digits 0 through 9
    vote_counts = tabulate(neighbor_labels + 1, nbins = 10)
    
    # If there is a voting tie, choose the smallest digit
    predictions[i] = which(vote_counts == max(vote_counts))[1] - 1
  }
  
  predictions
}
  1. Apply the classifier to all 500 test images using each distance. Keep all digit labels from 0 through 9 in the matrix, including any with a zero count. Which digits are most often confused with one another?

most_confused_pairs = function(cm, top_n = 5) {
  
  results = data.frame(
    Digit_1 = numeric(0),
    Digit_2 = numeric(0),
    Count = numeric(0)
  )
  
  for (digit1 in 0:8) {
    for (digit2 in (digit1 + 1):9) {
      
      count = cm[as.character(digit1), as.character(digit2)] +
        cm[as.character(digit2), as.character(digit1)]
      
      results = rbind(
        results,
        data.frame(
          Digit_1 = digit1,
          Digit_2 = digit2,
          Count = count
        )
      )
    }
  }
  
  results = results[order(-results$Count), ]
  head(results, top_n)
}

Question 5: Create a plot-formatting skill

Create a short SKILL.md file for improving the formatting of STAT 432 homework plots. You may use AI to help write it.

  1. Include a title, a description, and a few formatting rules. The description should limit the skill to STAT 432 homework plot improvements and require an explicit request to use it. Your rules should address margins, titles, axes, labels, colors, and sizes for plots produced in R or Python. Keep them portable: do not refer to specific homework questions.

• Solution:

---
name: stat432-plot-formatting
description: Improve the appearance and readability of STAT 432 homework plots only when the user explicitly asks to use this skill.
---

# STAT 432 Plot Formatting

- Keep the original data, calculations, statistical results, and meaning unchanged.
- Set margins so titles, axis labels, tick labels, and legends are fully visible and not crowded.
- Use concise titles that clearly describe what the plot shows.
- Make axes easy to read with clear labels, appropriate limits, and sensible tick spacing.
- Use descriptive axis labels and include measurement units when they are relevant.
- Use distinct, readable colors when comparing multiple curves or groups, while keeping the overall appearance simple.
- Choose text, point, and line sizes that remain readable when the plot is displayed in a homework document.
- Use a moderate figure size that fits naturally in an R Markdown or Python document without being too large or too small.
- Keep legends readable and place them where they do not cover important parts of the plot.
- Apply these improvements to the user's existing R or Python plotting code without changing the underlying analysis.
  1. Ask your agent to install the skill. Explicitly call it to improve the plot from Question 1, then compare the original and revised versions. Do you like the changes? You may revise the skill and test it a couple more times, or uninstall it if it remains unhelpful.

• Solution:

I installed stat432-plot-formatting and explicitly asked the agent to use it on the bias–variance plot from Question 1. The simulation results below are unchanged; only the presentation is revised.

Original version

Show the workflow 
plot(
  k.values, bias.squared,
  type = "l", lwd = 2,
  col = "darkorange",
  xlab = "k",
  ylab = "Error",
  ylim = range(c(bias.squared, variance, mse))
)

lines(k.values, variance,
      lwd = 2, col = "deepskyblue")

lines(k.values, mse,
      lwd = 2, col = "black")

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Squared Bias", "Variance", "MSE"),
  col = c("darkorange", "deepskyblue", "black"),
  lty = 1,
  lwd = 2
)

Revised version

Show the workflow 
old.par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mar = c(5.0, 5.2, 3.5, 8.0))

plot(
  k.values, bias.squared,
  type = "n",
  xlab = "Number of neighbors (k)",
  ylab = "Estimated squared error",
  main = expression("KNN Bias-Variance Trade-off at " * x[0]),
  xaxt = "n",
  ylim = c(0, max(mse) * 1.05),
  cex.main = 1.15,
  cex.lab = 1.05,
  cex.axis = 0.9
)

axis(1, at = seq(1, 29, by = 4), cex.axis = 0.9)
abline(h = pretty(c(0, max(mse))), col = "grey90", lwd = 0.8)

lines(k.values, bias.squared,
      type = "o", pch = 16, lty = 2, lwd = 2.2,
      cex = 0.75, col = "#D55E00")

lines(k.values, variance,
      type = "o", pch = 17, lty = 3, lwd = 2.2,
      cex = 0.75, col = "#0072B2")

lines(k.values, mse,
      type = "o", pch = 15, lty = 1, lwd = 2.4,
      cex = 0.7, col = "#222222")

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Squared Bias", "Variance", "MSE"),
  col = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#222222"),
  lty = 1,
  lwd = 2
)

box()
Show the workflow 
par(old.par)

I prefer the revised version. The title explains the statistical comparison, the axis labels are more descriptive, and the tick spacing is less crowded. The colorblind-friendly orange, blue, and black palette is reinforced by different line types and point symbols, so the curves remain distinguishable without relying only on color. The larger margins keep the labels visible, and moving the legend outside the plotting region prevents it from covering the data. These changes improve readability without changing the estimates or the bias–variance conclusion, so I kept the skill as written.

• Solution:

---
name: stat432-plot-formatting
description: Improve the appearance and readability of STAT 432 homework plots only when the user explicitly asks to use this skill.
---

# STAT 432 Plot Formatting

- Keep the original data, calculations, statistical results, and meaning unchanged.
- Set margins so titles, axis labels, tick labels, and legends are fully visible and not crowded.
- Use concise titles that clearly describe what the plot shows.
- Make axes easy to read with clear labels, appropriate limits, and sensible tick spacing.
- Use descriptive axis labels and include measurement units when they are relevant.
- Use distinct, readable colors when comparing multiple curves or groups, while keeping the overall appearance simple.
- Choose text, point, and line sizes that remain readable when the plot is displayed in a homework document.
- Use a moderate figure size that fits naturally in an R Markdown or Python document without being too large or too small.

I limited the skill to STAT 432 homework plots and required an explicit request so that it does not change plots during unrelated work. The rules focus on readability while protecting the statistical content: the data, calculations, and meaning must remain unchanged. I also kept the instructions portable so they can be applied to either R or Python plotting code.

The skill was helpful when revising the Question 1 plot. It produced clearer labels, a descriptive title, more readable line and point sizes, and colors and line types that make the curves easier to distinguish. During the first test, the legend text extended beyond the figure boundary. I reduced the legend offset and rendered the document again, which kept the legend outside the data region while making it fully visible. After that adjustment, I was satisfied with the result and kept the skill installed.
